summary: Describes a convention for escaping Unicode characters in ASCII text where they cannot be sent directly. It is a Best Current Practice document.

eli5.summary: Some places can only handle basic letters. This is a standard way to write other letters, like accented ones, using only basic characters.

questions: how to escape unicode in ascii
what is a unicode code point escape
should i use utf-8 octets or code points for escapes
subtitle: How Internet protocols should write Unicode characters using only ASCII, and which escape syntaxes to prefer.

tldr.problem: Protocols often need to carry characters they cannot send directly, and Unicode, with its several encodings, has produced many competing escape syntaxes.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends escaping by Unicode code point in hexadecimal rather than by UTF-8 or UTF-16 octets, and recommends two delimited forms: backslash-u with quotes, and the XML style ampersand-hash-x form.
tldr.outcome: It does not mandate one syntax. Protocols that use escapes MUST define their own, and should avoid decimal, octal and surrogate-pair forms.

today: RFC 5137 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 137) document published in February 2008. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Unicode Escapes Are Needed
sections.content:
Sometimes a protocol needs an escape mechanism to carry characters that cannot be represented or transmitted directly. With ASCII, the traditional escape was the decimal or hexadecimal value of the character, written many ways. The RFC lists examples such as %dNN, %xNN, X'nn' and %X'NN', notes that %NN became popular through URLs, and mentions MIME Quoted-Printable and Encoded-word as yet other escapes.

Unicode complicates this because characters occupy two or more octets and can be coded several ways. Code points run from 0 to hex 10FFFF and are written in text as U+0000 to U+10FFFF. Serialized, they can be UTF-8 with one to four octets, UTF-16 with two or four octets, or UTF-32 with exactly four.

New protocols that carry text for humans SHOULD allow the full Unicode repertoire (per RFC 2277). This RFC says existing protocols being internationalized, and those that need an escape mechanism, SHOULD use some contextually appropriate variation on code point references. It does not apply to protocols that already accept native UTF-8 or another Unicode encoding, where accepting those forms is preferable.
sections.eli5: Long ago people wrote special letters in many different secret ways. Now there are even more letters, so this RFC helps everyone pick a tidy way to write them down.

sections.title: Code Points Versus UTF-8 or UTF-16 Octets
sections.content:
There are two main families of Unicode escapes. One writes the code point, the other writes the octets of an encoding such as UTF-8. The RFC says code points SHOULD be used rather than UTF-8 or UTF-16 octets, in the absence of compelling reasons.

  • Human-readable text is a reason for the success of many IETF protocols, and a code point can be looked up in the Unicode tables directly.
  • Reading UTF-8 octets requires decoding steps before a code point can be found, which makes errors more likely and debugging harder.
  • Except for ASCII (U+0000 through U+007F), the code point form is generally more compact, sometimes much more.

The same considerations apply to compact ACE encodings such as bootstring and its Punycode profile. They also apply to UTF-16 forms such as Java's \uNNNN: these match code points inside the Basic Multilingual Plane, but higher planes need surrogates and a two-stage decoding process.
sections.eli5: It is easier to say 'the letter in box number 233' than to spell out how the letter is packed into bytes. Box numbers are quick to look up.

sections.title: Referring to Characters in Text
sections.content: Separately from escapes inside protocols, the RFC addresses prose. Text that refers to a Unicode code point SHOULD use the U+NNNN[N[N]] syntax from the Unicode Standard, where the digits are hexadecimal. Text that actually contains a Unicode character SHOULD use a syntax better suited to automated processing.
sections.eli5: When you talk about a letter, say its number with a U+ in front. When you really want the letter itself, use a form a computer can read.

sections.title: Choosing a Syntax for Code Point Escapes
sections.content:
All code point escapes are equivalent in meaning. They differ only in syntax, and the best choice depends on where it is used. Two rules are firm: hexadecimal is preferable, so systems based on decimal or octal offsets SHOULD NOT be used, and protocol specifications that use escapes MUST define their syntax, including how to write the escape sequence literally.

The RFC offers factors to weigh:

  • Consistency with related protocols that already use a form.
  • Code points can need four, five, six or eight hex digits, so forms with explicit delimiters are generally preferred, and symmetric paired delimiters are easier to recognize.
  • Forms starting with \u and no delimiters are used by C, Java and others with different digit counts, which invites confusion.
  • Forms that need surrogate pairs share the problems of UTF-8 octets, and Internet protocols SHOULD NOT use them.
sections.eli5: Any numbered-box system works as long as it is spelled out clearly. Brackets around the number help you see where it starts and stops.

sections.title: The Two Recommended Forms
sections.content:
Two forms are recommended for Internet protocols.

The first is backslash-u with delimiters: a lowercase \u, an apostrophe, four to six hexadecimal digits, and a closing apostrophe. Designers using it should specify how to escape the introducing backslash; \\ is one obvious option.

The second is the XML form &#xNNNN;, with two to six hex digits and a closing semicolon. HTML uses a similar form, but the semicolon may be omitted in some cases. The RFC says the HTML form without the semicolon SHOULD NOT be used, since the delimiter's advantage disappears. It also admits this style is often seen as ugly outside HTML and XML. A literal ampersand is written & in this style.
sections.eli5: The first way wraps the number in quote marks. The second starts with a few symbols and ends with a semicolon. Both make it obvious where the number ends.

sections.title: Forms Normally Not Recommended
sections.content:
Three popular forms are discouraged, with their formal syntax in the appendix (which is not normative).

  • C: \uNNNN for plane 0 and \UNNNNNNNN for any character. The upper and lower case difference may seem unnatural, and the many conventions starting with \u breed confusion.
  • Perl: \x{NNNN...}. It has explicit delimiters, but values from \x(00) through \x(FF) may be read as the local character set, so it should be used with extreme caution, if at all.
  • Java: \uNNNN, which refers to UTF-16 values, not code points. Outside plane 0 it needs surrogate pairs, so it SHOULD NOT be used as an escape except where natural in Java.
sections.eli5: Some programming languages have their own ways. They work in their own worlds, but they can be mixed up with each other, so the RFC says to be careful.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because the recommended encodings are unambiguous and normalization is not involved, the RFC expects no security issues beyond those from using non-ASCII characters at all. Making the identity of characters somewhat more obvious should slightly lower the risk of confusing users.

It also warns that an escape mechanism allows a character to be represented in more than one way. Where software interprets the escaped form, security checks, and checks for minimal or normalized forms, might be done at the wrong point.
sections.eli5: If one letter can be written two ways, a guard checking the wrong version might be fooled. So check at the right moment.
